title: What Decipherment Requires
description: The conditions that make breaking an unknown script possible — and the ones that make it impossible

concepts.title: Three Things You Need
concepts.contentHtml:
To decipher an unknown script you generally need three things at once: a known underlying language (or a good guess at one), a sufficient corpus (so signs repeat enough to analyse), and ideally a bilingual artefact (the same text in your script and a known one).

The Rosetta Stone gave Champollion all three for Egyptian hieroglyphs — Greek + Demotic + hieroglyphs in parallel, with Coptic as the still-spoken descendant of the underlying language. Linear B fell when Michael Ventris guessed the language was an early Greek and exploited a corpus of clay-tablet inventories.

Lacking even one of these, decipherment becomes mathematically underdetermined.

concepts.title: Why It's Hard
concepts.contentHtml:
An unknown script-language pair is roughly an underconstrained substitution cipher with an unknown plaintext language. If the language is unknown and there's no bilingual, you cannot uniquely recover meaning — every grammar consistent with the corpus is a valid candidate.

The corpus matters because letter and bigram frequencies stabilise only with enough text. The Indus script's corpus is short — average inscription is ~5 signs, the longest ~26. Statistical signatures barely emerge.

Some unknown scripts may not encode language at all — they could be tally marks, symbol systems for ritual or property, or hybrid systems mixing logographic with phonetic elements.

concepts.title: Why People Keep Trying
concepts.contentHtml:
Each undeciphered script is a sealed window into a literate society. Decipherment instantly multiplies what we know about that civilisation. Linear B's break revealed Mycenaean palace inventories, names of gods, geography. Maya's break (mostly between 1950–80) opened a continent of preserved history.

The rewards are large enough that amateur and academic effort is continuous. The risk is that wrong decipherments are publishable too — Voynich has had dozens of declared 'solutions' that quietly fail to reproduce on review.

title: Linear A
description: The Minoan script that hid behind its successor

concepts.title: The Minoans Wrote It
concepts.contentHtml:
Linear A was the writing system of the Minoan civilisation on Crete from roughly 1800–1450 BCE. About 1,400 known inscriptions exist, mostly on small clay tablets, fragmentary and short. The corpus is enough to identify ~90 distinct signs but not enough for confident phonetic assignment.

Linear A is the parent script of Linear B, which the Mycenaean Greeks adapted from it around 1450 BCE. Linear B was famously deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952 — and Linear B documents an early form of Greek.

concepts.title: The Sound-Value Trap
concepts.contentHtml:
Because Linear B and Linear A share many sign shapes, scholars have tried assigning Linear B's known sound values to identical Linear A signs and reading the result. The output is gibberish in every known language. The Minoan language is not Greek, not Indo-European, not Semitic, not anything reconstructed.

This is informative: it tells us Linear A encoded a language unrelated to its successor — the Mycenaeans inherited the script but spoke something else entirely. The language behind Linear A is sometimes called Eteocretan ('true Cretan') and remains a linguistic isolate.

concepts.title: What Might Crack It
concepts.contentHtml:
A bilingual artefact would crack it instantly. None has been found despite extensive Cretan archaeology. A long enough monoglot text might allow statistical attack if assumptions about ancient Mediterranean phonotactics are imposed — work continues.

Computational approaches (Hidden Markov Models, neural-net acoustic regularities, character-embedding alignment with related scripts) have made small progress. As of 2026 some signs have probable phonetic readings, but no full decipherment is accepted by consensus.

title: The Indus Script
description: Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, and inscriptions too short to break

concepts.title: The Civilisation
concepts.contentHtml:
The Indus Valley Civilisation (roughly 2600–1900 BCE) covered modern Pakistan and northwest India — cities like Mohenjo-daro and Harappa with planned grids, sewerage, standardised brick sizes, and a script we cannot read. About 4,000 inscribed objects survive: stamp seals, copper tablets, pottery shards.

The inscriptions are characteristically short. Average length is around 5 signs. The longest known continuous text is 17 signs on a single line, 26 in total across one object. Total corpus: ~400 distinct signs across all 4,000 inscriptions.

concepts.title: Is It Even Language?
concepts.contentHtml:
The shortness has triggered a serious debate: is Indus script writing at all? Steve Farmer and colleagues argued in 2004 that the inscriptions might be heraldic, ritual, or property symbols rather than encoded speech. Average length is far shorter than in scripts known to encode language.

Counter-arguments from Asko Parpola and others rely on positional regularities (certain signs only at the start, others only at the end) which look linguistic. Statistical analyses of conditional sign frequencies (Rao et al. 2009) show structure consistent with language. The debate is unresolved.

If it isn't a script, no decipherment is possible because there's nothing to decipher.

concepts.title: Candidate Languages
concepts.contentHtml:
If Indus is a script, the underlying language is unknown. The most-discussed candidates: Proto-Dravidian (south Indian language family, supported by Asko Parpola); Proto-Indo-European / early Indo-Aryan (politically charged in modern India, less linguistically supported); a now-extinct isolate.

Without bilingual finds and with such a short corpus, statistical attack is structurally limited. The same set of signs is consistent with multiple language hypotheses. The Indus script may remain undeciphered indefinitely.

title: The Voynich Manuscript
description: An early-15th-century book in a script no one has read

concepts.title: What It Is
concepts.contentHtml:
The Voynich Manuscript is a hand-written book on parchment, radiocarbon-dated to roughly 1404–1438 CE. It contains ~240 surviving pages of unknown script, illustrated with botanical drawings (often depicting non-existent plants), naked figures in tubs connected by piping, astrological diagrams, and dense paragraphs of text.

It was named for the bookseller Wilfrid Voynich who acquired it in 1912. The manuscript is now at Yale's Beinecke Library (MS 408). Its provenance before the 17th century is unclear; it appears in 17th-century correspondence as already-undecipherable.

concepts.title: Voynichese Has Linguistic Structure
concepts.contentHtml:
The script — called 'Voynichese' — has 20–30 distinct characters. Statistical analysis shows it behaves like natural language: Zipf's law word-frequency distribution, structured letter-position rules, sections with measurably different vocabularies (botanical pages use one word-set, astrological pages another).

This is hard to fake. Random gibberish doesn't naturally produce Zipfian statistics. A medieval forger would have had to know about statistical regularities four centuries before they were articulated. Either Voynichese encodes a real language, an artificial language with linguistic-quality structure, or a sophisticated cipher whose ciphertext mimics Zipf — all interesting possibilities.

concepts.title: Failed Solutions
concepts.contentHtml:
Voynich has been 'solved' dozens of times. Every solution fails on review: it explains the first few words plausibly then collapses, can't predict any new word, or relies on circular reasoning. Recent claimed solutions invoking medieval Hebrew, proto-Romance, Manchu, Old Turkic, and others have all failed reproducibility.

Two stable conclusions remain: the manuscript was made in early-15th-century Europe (carbon-dating + ink + parchment); and Voynichese has more linguistic structure than random nonsense. Beyond that, the field is open. As of 2026 there is no consensus solution.

title: Rongorongo and the Rest
description: Easter Island's script and other unbroken systems

concepts.title: Rongorongo
concepts.contentHtml:
Rongorongo is a script found on ~25 carved wooden tablets from Rapa Nui (Easter Island). It was apparently developed by the Rapanui civilisation. By the time European missionaries arrived in 1864 the literate population had collapsed from disease and slave raids — the script was effectively lost within a generation.

The script reads in reverse boustrophedon: alternating lines flipped top-to-bottom. About 120 distinct glyphs combine into ~480 compound symbols. The total corpus is small. The underlying Rapa Nui language is known (a Polynesian language), but no bilingual exists and 19th-century informants gave conflicting readings.

concepts.title: Cretan Hieroglyphic and Proto-Elamite
concepts.contentHtml:
Cretan hieroglyphic predates Linear A on Crete (c. 2100–1700 BCE). It has its own undeciphered set of ~100 signs. Whether it encodes the same language as Linear A is unclear.

Proto-Elamite (Iran, c. 3100–2900 BCE) is the earliest writing system from the Iranian plateau. It has ~1,000 distinct signs across ~1,600 tablets. Its underlying language ('Proto-Elamite') is hypothesized to be the ancestor of Elamite (which was deciphered) but the connection cannot be confirmed without breaking Proto-Elamite first — circular.

Each of these scripts has the same combination of constraints: short corpus, no bilingual, unknown language relationship. Each remains effectively unbreakable.

concepts.title: What This Tells Us About Knowledge
concepts.contentHtml:
Roughly a dozen ancient scripts remain undeciphered. Each represents a literate population whose words cannot be read. Most will likely never be cracked: bilingual artefacts come from chance, and chance has been kind in some cases (Rosetta, Behistun) but absent in others.

Modern computational methods help with statistical structure but cannot conjure missing constraints. A short corpus in an unknown language is mathematically underdetermined regardless of compute. The lower bound on what we can know is sometimes simply zero.

Information once written, then lost, can be permanently lost. The undeciphered scripts are a memento for any culture that thinks its records are forever.
